fields.citation: Basil of Caesarea, Hexaemeron, Homily 2.8 (on Genesis 1:5)
fields.note: The homily reasons that Scripture says “one day” rather than “the first day” in order to fix the measure of day and night together: “Now twenty-four hours fill up the space of one day — we mean of a day and of a night.” Basil reads the day as ordinary time; other Fathers, including Origen, read the days non-literally, and no Orthodox council has dogmatized the question.

fields.citation: Answers in Genesis, Statement of Faith, “Origins and History” section
fields.note: The statement says: “The days in Genesis do not correspond to geologic ages but are six consecutive, 24-hour days of creation.” A young-earth reading is common within the tradition's more conservative wing, though the Baptist Faith and Message does not itself specify.

fields.citation: Creation Research Society, Statement of Belief, point 1
fields.note: The statement says: “The Bible is the written Word of God, and because it is inspired throughout, all its assertions are historically and scientifically true in the original autographs. To the student of nature this means that the account of origins in Genesis is a factual presentation of simple historical truths.” See the tradition override below for how this position relates to the cosmic-temple reading within the same stream.

fields.citation: BioLogos, Faith Commitments (2024 revision of “What We Believe”)
fields.note: BioLogos affirms evolution, including common descent, as the best scientific explanation for the diversity of life over billions of years, held together with a Christ-centered, biblical faith (“Rigorous Science” and “Christ-centered Faith” among its three stated core values). The page was rewritten in 2024 into a shorter statement; the corpus's earlier “articles 1-12” numbering no longer applies.
